en: The Garland of the Nine Jewels of Dakṣiṇāmūrti Hymn of Praise.
Bearing a few locks of hair tawny like a golden chisel, wearing a mass of matted locks as fierce as brown snakes,
with a forehead smiling with the smear of ashes— the slayer of Smara was seen at the foot of a banyan tree, destroying the evil of forgetfulness.
Beneath the *nyagrodha* tree, his neck was as majestic as a cloud that has surpassed its depth, and his great coil of matted hair was like a fitting ornament for a multitude of serpents.
We contemplate Him who has the form of a youth, who wears the charming moon as His crest-ornament, whose gentle smile brings an end to delusion, and who is the cessation of all infatuation.

My inner mind is rendered wondrous by the power of Citkalā—who, with Her lotus-like face, possesses a mass of matted hair tawny like a swarm of bees upon the filaments of that lotus; and who, through the sight bestowed from Her nose, possesses the strength to laugh at the great epilepsy of pride and to devour the god of death.

My mind is fixed upon that mountain-peak of knowledge, sought by poets, which wears the Vedas as its garland and whose crest-jewel is the dancing river (Gaṅgā); it is fixed upon that forehead-fire of intense egoism, which has consumed the god of love.
[4] He who has fashioned a waist-cloth from a tiger-skin and a variegated cloth, and who is the ocean of wisdom for the commentaries on the words of the Vedas—
The golden cleverness of consciousness, the mother of liberation and the root of boundless majesty, shines within my mind.

I worship the Lord Bhava, who has the moon as his crest-jewel, a dark throat, an eye on his forehead, vermilion lips, and a pure body; who is encircled by the lord of serpents, whose laughter glows with the splendor of the sun, and who wears a tiger skin as his garment.

May that certain wisdom-mudrā of the Sage—who is like the sun to the destruction of the darkness of delusion—constantly sever our suffering as it rests upon the heart; she who lies upon the root-ground of the Nyagrodha tree.
She is white as frost, water, a pearl necklace, Airāvata, the Gaṅgā, a row of sandalwood trees, sacred ash, nectar, and the moon.

I worship that peaceful splendor, the greatness of which is my Guru—within whom there is no blinking of the eyes, yet who wears a garland of six-fold rudrākṣa beads; who possesses a gentle smile and is beginningless;
whose one foot is planted upon the broad back of a fierce, unconscious elephant, while his other foot rests upon its massive thigh;
and whose body is rendered motionless through the contemplation of the ultimate reality.
That fortunate person who, freed from dullness, daily recites with devotion this garland consisting of nine jewels to the Primordial Guru,
attains equality with the forty-eight thousand [verses] and indeed merges into Him.
Thus ends the *Dakṣiṇāmūrtinavaratnamālikāstotra*, composed by the illustrious Navanāthasiddha.
